title: The Old Man Who Planted a Fig Tree
summary: The emperor Hadrian meets a man a hundred years old who is planting a fig tree, and asks him why he bothers. The old man's answer, "Just as my ancestors worked for me, so I work for my children," teaches about gratitude to the generations before us and caring for the generations after us.
pages:
One morning, on a dusty road, a great king passed by with many soldiers.
It was the emperor Hadrian, and he was riding a tall white horse.

Suddenly the king stopped. By the side of the road stood a very old man with a long white beard.
The old man was digging a small hole in the ground, slowly, slowly, and planting a fig tree sapling in it.

"Grandpa," called the king, "how old are you?"
The old man wiped his forehead and smiled. "I am a hundred years old," he answered.

The king raised his eyebrows. "A hundred? And you're still working hard and planting trees?
A fig tree grows slowly. Do you think you'll live to eat from it?"

The old man stroked the little sapling. "If I'm lucky, I'll eat from it," he said. "And if not, that's all right.
Just as my ancestors worked for me, so I work for my children."

What does that mean? The old man explained:
"When I was a boy, I ate figs from trees my grandfather planted. Now I am planting for my children and grandchildren."

The king was quiet and thought. "If you live to eat from this tree," he said, "come and tell me."
Then he went on his way with all his soldiers.

Years passed. The sapling grew into a wide tree, with big green leaves.
And one day sweet, soft, purple figs ripened on it.

The old man filled a basket with figs and went to the palace.
"My lord the king, I am the old man who planted the fig tree. Look, I lived to eat from it!"

The king was very happy. He sat the old man on a golden chair and filled his basket with shining gold coins.
"You deserve honor," he said, "because you worked hard for others too."

You, too, eat fruit from trees that someone planted long, long ago.
And maybe tomorrow you'll plant a little seed, and someone else will eat from it and smile.
